name: USING YOUR RIGHTS
safetyNote: Using this right is legal, but a stop can still get tense. Stay calm, keep your hands where the officer can see them, and do not run or argue. If an officer tells you to do something, do it, and then say your words again. Getting home safe comes first. You fight an unfair stop later, in court, with a lawyer.

questions.q: What is the best way to use your right to remain silent?

options.text: Say the words out loud: "I am using my right to remain silent." Then stay quiet.
Just stay quiet. Not answering is the same thing as using the right.
options.explanation: This feels true but it is not. The Supreme Court says staying quiet by itself does not turn the right on. You have to say it. If you only stay quiet, police can keep asking questions for hours, and if you crack and answer even one, that answer counts.

options.text: Answer the easy questions and skip the ones that could get you in trouble.
options.explanation: There are no easy questions. Everything you say can be used, including the answers that feel harmless. Answering some questions also keeps the conversation going, and it can look like you chose to talk.

options.text: Stay quiet, but only if you really did nothing wrong. Going silent when you were there makes you look guilty.
options.explanation: Using your right cannot be used against you. A prosecutor is not allowed to tell a jury that staying silent means you did it. Innocent people use this right all the time, because talking is how you accidentally say something wrong even when you did nothing.

questions.hint: Rights are like a light switch. Does this one turn on by itself, or do you have to flip it?
questions.principle: Here is the strange part of this right: staying silent is not enough to use your right to stay silent. You have to say it out loud. The Supreme Court decided this in a case called Berghuis v. Thompkins in 2010. A man named Van Chester Thompkins sat through almost three hours of questions and said almost nothing. Near the end, an officer asked if he prayed to God for forgiveness for the shooting. He said "yes." That one word helped convict him, because he never said he was using his right. Once you clearly say you are staying silent, the questions about the case have to stop. The words turn the right on. Silence alone does not.

keyPhrase.quote: I am using my right to remain silent.
keyPhrase.gloss: Say it clearly, then stop talking. These words are what make the questions stop.

scenario.setup: You are on the sidewalk outside the park. An officer walks up.

lines.label: OFFICER
lines.text: Were you at the park earlier? I just need to know who was there.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: I am using my right to remain silent.

lines.label: OFFICER
lines.text: I am not accusing you. Just tell me who else was around.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: I am using my right to remain silent. I want a lawyer.

lines.label: YES
lines.text: You said the words and repeated them. Questions about the case have to stop. Nothing you said can hurt you, because you never said anything about the case.

lines.label: NO
lines.text: You stayed quiet but never said the words. He keeps asking for an hour. You finally say "I was there but I didn't do anything." That sentence puts you at the park, and it counts.

scenario.note: Saying it twice is not rude. Officers are trained to keep asking, and repeating it is how you show you meant it.

questions.q: Which of these actually turns on your right to a lawyer?

options.text: "I want a lawyer."
"Maybe I should talk to a lawyer?"
options.explanation: A maybe is not a request. The Supreme Court decided that a hedge like this does not count, and police do not even have to stop and ask what you meant. They can keep questioning you.

options.text: "I'd want a lawyer, but we can't pay for one."
options.explanation: You get a lawyer for free if your family cannot afford one. That is true in juvenile court too. Ask first and let the court sort out who pays.

options.text: "I want a lawyer, but I'll keep answering until they get here."
options.explanation: Asking for a lawyer only helps if you also stop talking. Once you ask, questioning has to stop, but if you keep talking anyway, those answers still count.

questions.hint: One of these is a question, one is a guess, and one is a request. Which one leaves nothing to interpret?
questions.principle: Asking for a lawyer only works if you say it clearly. In 1994 the Supreme Court decided a case called Davis v. United States. A man being questioned said "Maybe I should talk to a lawyer." The agents did not stop. They were not even required to ask him what he meant. He kept talking, and what he said was used against him. Later he said clearly that he wanted a lawyer, and only then did questioning stop. The rule is that a maybe, a question, or a hint does not count. Say it flat: "I want a lawyer." Then stop talking and wait.

keyPhrase.quote: I want a lawyer. Not maybe. Not I think.
keyPhrase.gloss: Say it flat. A hedge does not count.

scenario.setup: You are in a small room at the station. You are nervous and not sure what to say.

lines.label: OFFICER
lines.text: So walk me through your night.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: Maybe I should talk to a lawyer?

lines.label: OFFICER
lines.text: That's up to you. So anyway, where were you around nine?

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: I want a lawyer. I am not answering questions.

lines.label: YES
lines.text: The second time, there was nothing to guess about. Questions have to stop.

lines.label: NO
lines.text: You only ever said maybe. That is not clear enough, so the officer keeps going, and everything you say next counts.

scenario.note: Do not soften it. This is the one moment where being blunt protects you.

questions.q: An officer tells you your friend already confessed and blamed you. What is true about that?

options.text: Police are allowed to lie about evidence during questioning.
Police have to be truthful when they question someone.
options.explanation: Courts have allowed police to lie about evidence for a long time. They can say they have your fingerprints, a video, or a confession that does not exist. It is legal, and it works.

options.text: They can only say it if your friend actually said it.
options.explanation: They do not need proof, because they do not need it to be true. It can work whether or not anyone actually talked.

options.text: Saying it is allowed, but anything you say afterward gets thrown out.
options.explanation: A statement you give after being lied to usually still counts. That is what makes this dangerous. The lie is legal and your answer is still evidence.

questions.hint: Is something being unfair the same as it being against the rules?
questions.principle: Police are allowed to lie to you while questioning you. They can say a friend confessed, that they have video, or that your fingerprints are on something, even when none of it is true. Courts have allowed this for a long time. Being told that someone else already talked is common during questioning, and it is convincing because it makes talking feel pointless. Here is what matters: none of it changes what you should do. If you have said you are staying silent and you want a lawyer, that is still the answer. A lie cannot be used against you. Your response to it can.

keyPhrase.quote: Whatever they say they have, my answer is the same.
keyPhrase.gloss: A lie cannot hurt you. What you say back can.

scenario.setup: You already said you were staying silent. The officer comes back into the room holding a folder.

lines.label: OFFICER
lines.text: Your buddy already told us the whole thing. He says it was your idea.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: I am still not answering questions.

lines.label: OFFICER
lines.text: He's helping himself right now. This is your last chance to tell your side.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: I am still not answering questions. I want a lawyer.

lines.label: YES
lines.text: You never find out whether the friend said anything, and it does not matter. Nothing new came from you.

lines.label: NO
lines.text: You say "it wasn't my idea, he's the one who wanted to." You have just put yourself there and confirmed it happened.

scenario.note: There is usually no deadline like that. Your side is something your lawyer helps you tell later, when you have had time to think.

questions.q: You have been answering an officer's questions for ten minutes. Can you stop now?

options.text: Yes. You can stop at any point, even in the middle of a conversation.
No. Once you start answering, you have to finish the conversation.
options.explanation: There is no rule that makes you finish. You can stop at any moment. The answers you already gave still count, but everything after you stop is protected.

options.text: Only if you have not said anything important yet.
options.explanation: It does not matter what you already said. Stopping is always available, and it is more useful the deeper in you are, not less.

options.text: Yes, but the officer has to agree to stop first.
options.explanation: You do not need permission. Once you clearly say you are done and want a lawyer, questioning has to stop.

questions.hint: Think about whether this is a door that locks behind you, or one you can walk back through.
questions.principle: You can stop talking at any time, even if you have already been answering for a while. There is no point where you have talked so much that stopping stops mattering. This matters because of how questioning usually goes. Almost nobody refuses from the very first second. People answer a few easy questions, then a few more, and by the time it turns serious they feel locked in. You are not locked in. Say that you are done answering and that you want a lawyer, and the questions have to stop. What you already said still counts, but you can stop it from getting worse.

keyPhrase.quote: I am done answering questions. I want a lawyer.
keyPhrase.gloss: You can say this at minute one or minute forty. It works the same.

scenario.setup: You have been talking for ten minutes. It started friendly. The questions just got sharper.

lines.label: OFFICER
lines.text: So you were at the store around six. Who was with you?

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: I am done answering questions. I want a lawyer.

lines.label: OFFICER
lines.text: You've been talking this whole time. Why stop now?

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: I am done answering questions.

lines.label: YES
lines.text: The last ten minutes still count, but the next hour never happens. That is the part that usually does the damage.

lines.label: NO
lines.text: You answer the harder questions too. Those are the ones most likely to be used as evidence, and they are the ones you could have skipped.

scenario.note: Feeling rude is not a legal problem. You are allowed to stop a conversation you agreed to start.

questions.q: You are being questioned and you ask for your mom. Does that stop the questioning?

options.text: No. Asking for a parent is not the same as asking for a lawyer.
Yes. Asking for a parent works the same as asking for a lawyer.
options.explanation: They are different requests. Asking for a lawyer is what makes questioning stop. Asking for a parent might get your parent called, but on its own it does not turn your rights on.

options.text: Yes, because police cannot question anyone under 18 without a parent there.
options.explanation: There is no rule that a parent has to be in the room. A parent may be notified, but questioning can happen without one present.

options.text: No, and once a parent arrives they can decide whether you talk.
options.explanation: The rights are yours, not your parent's. A parent cannot give up your right to stay silent for you, and they cannot make you talk.

questions.hint: Two different people, two different jobs. Which one is trained to protect you legally?
questions.principle: Asking for a parent and asking for a lawyer are not the same request, and only one of them makes questioning stop. This is one of the most common mistakes young people make, because asking for a parent is the natural thing to do. Your parent may be called, and having them there can help. But a parent is not a lawyer, cannot give legal advice, and cannot turn your rights on for you. It also works the other way: your parent cannot give up your rights for you either. Those rights are yours. If you want the questions to stop, the words that do it are "I want a lawyer." You can ask for both.

keyPhrase.quote: I want my mom, and I want a lawyer.
keyPhrase.gloss: Ask for both. Only one of them stops the questions.

scenario.setup: You are sixteen, in a room at the station, and you want your mom.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: Can you call my mom?

lines.label: OFFICER
lines.text: We'll get to that. First, tell me about the car.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: I want my mom, and I want a lawyer. I am not answering questions.

lines.label: OFFICER
lines.text: Okay.

lines.label: YES
lines.text: The lawyer request is what stops the questions. The parent request still gets your mom involved.

lines.label: NO
lines.text: Questioning can continue while you wait, and answers you give in that time count.

scenario.note: Even after a parent arrives, the rights are still yours. If your parent tells you to just explain, you can still say you want a lawyer.

questions.q: An officer says "this is off the record, just between us." What does that actually mean for you?

options.text: It means nothing. There is no such thing as off the record with police.
It means what you say cannot be used in court.
options.explanation: There is no off the record rule. An officer saying it does not make it true, and what you say can still be written down, repeated, and used.

options.text: It means you are safe as long as nothing is recorded or written down.
options.explanation: An officer can testify about what you said from memory or from notes made later. A conversation does not have to be recorded to count as evidence.

options.text: It means it only counts if you sign something afterward.
options.explanation: Nothing needs to be signed. A statement counts whether you signed it, wrote it, or only said it out loud.

questions.hint: Who decides what counts as evidence, the person talking to you or a court?
questions.principle: Off the record is not a real thing when you talk to police. No rule makes a talk disappear because someone called it casual. An officer can write down what you said later. They can also tell a court about it from memory. It does not matter if you signed anything. Studies found that about half of people thought off the record talk could not be used. About a quarter thought a statement had to be signed to count. Both are wrong. If you are talking to police, you are on the record.

keyPhrase.quote: There is no off the record.
keyPhrase.gloss: Written down or not, it all counts.

scenario.setup: The recorder is off and the conversation feels casual.

lines.label: OFFICER
lines.text: Look, off the record, I get it. Just tell me what really happened and we can move on.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: I am not answering questions. I want a lawyer.

lines.label: OFFICER
lines.text: I'm not writing any of this down.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: I am not answering questions.

lines.label: YES
lines.text: Nothing exists to write down later, because you did not say anything about the case.

lines.label: NO
lines.text: The officer can write it down afterward or describe it in court. The casual tone does not change what it is.

scenario.note: A relaxed conversation is still a conversation with police. Nothing about the tone changes the rules.

questions.q: Your friend texts you from the police station: "they said if I just explain it I can go home tonight." What is the best thing to text back?

options.text: "Say you want a lawyer and stop talking. Ask them to call your parents."
"Just tell the truth, you didn't do anything wrong so it'll be fine."
options.explanation: Being innocent does not make talking safe. People who did nothing wrong still say things that get used against them, because they are scared, guessing, or trying to be helpful.

options.text: "Tell them the parts that make you look good and leave the rest out."
options.explanation: A half story is still a statement. Leaving parts out can also make it look like you were hiding something once the rest comes out.

options.text: "Ask them to promise in writing you can go home first, then explain."
options.explanation: An officer cannot promise what happens to your case, and a promise like that would not bind the court anyway. Whether you go home is not decided by the person questioning you.

questions.hint: Your friend is being offered a trade. Who actually has the power to deliver the thing being offered?
questions.principle: Tell us and you can go home is a hard thing to hear. It is also one of the least reliable. The officer asking you does not decide if you get charged. Other people make that call later. Talking almost never speeds things up. It often adds to the case against you. More than nine out of ten young people give up their rights when asked. A big reason is that they think talking is the fast way out. Asking for a lawyer does not promise you go home. It does put someone on your side in the room first.

keyPhrase.quote: Ask for a lawyer, then stop talking.
keyPhrase.gloss: This is the right answer whether you did something or not.

scenario.setup: Your phone buzzes. It is your friend, from the station.

lines.label: FRIEND
lines.text: they said if i just explain it i can go home tonight

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: don't explain anything. say "I want a lawyer" and stop talking

lines.label: FRIEND
lines.text: but i didn't even do anything

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: doesn't matter. say it anyway. ask them to call your parents

lines.label: YES
lines.text: Questioning stops. Whether they go home gets decided by people who were never in that room.

lines.label: NO
lines.text: They may still not go home, and now there is a statement in the file that a lawyer has to work around.

scenario.note: Wanting to go home is the most normal thing in the world. It is also the feeling that leads to most statements.

questions.q: An officer starts asking you questions and you are not sure whether you have to stay. What is the most useful thing to ask?

options.text: "Am I free to leave?"
"Did I do something wrong?"
options.explanation: This is the most natural thing to ask, but it does not tell you whether you can go, and it opens a longer conversation instead of a shorter one.

options.text: "Do you have a warrant?"
options.explanation: Warrants are for searches and arrests. An officer does not need one to walk up and talk to you, so the answer tells you nothing about your situation.

options.text: "What am I being charged with?"
options.explanation: Charges are filed later by a prosecutor, not by the officer in front of you. There may be no charges at all.

questions.hint: You want to know one thing: can you walk away? Which of these asks that directly?
questions.principle: Most conversations with police are ordinary. Officers talk to people all day for reasons that have nothing to do with suspicion, and there is nothing wrong with a normal conversation. But sometimes you cannot tell whether you are chatting or being held, and the two start exactly the same way. One question sorts it out: "Am I free to leave?" You can also ask "Am I being detained?" They mean the same thing. If the answer is yes, you can go. If the answer is no, you are being held, and that is the moment when staying silent and asking for a lawyer matter most. Asking is polite and it is not an admission of anything.

keyPhrase.quote: Am I free to leave?
keyPhrase.gloss: Or "Am I being detained?" Same question. The answer tells you which situation you are in.

scenario.setup: You are waiting outside a store for your ride. An officer walks over and starts talking.

lines.label: OFFICER
lines.text: How's it going? You waiting on somebody?

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: Am I free to leave?

lines.label: OFFICER
lines.text: Sure, you're not in any trouble. Just checking in.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: Okay, thanks. My ride's almost here.

lines.label: YES
lines.text: Nothing bad happened. You found out where you stand, and you can stay and chat or go, whichever you want.

lines.label: NO
lines.text: If the answer had been no, you would know it is serious, and you would know to say you want a lawyer.

scenario.note: Asking works in both directions. Most of the time the answer is yes, and the conversation stays friendly.

questions.q: Police arrest you and never read you your rights. What does that mean for your case?

options.text: Not much on its own. It mainly affects whether things you said can be used.
The case gets thrown out.
options.explanation: Not reading rights does not cancel a case. Other evidence like video, witnesses, or property usually still counts, and the case can go forward. It is only in rare situations, where the statements were the whole case, that charges get dropped.

options.text: Nothing you say counts, since they never read your rights.
options.explanation: It is narrower than that. The warning matters for questioning after you are in custody. Things you volunteer without being questioned can still count.

options.text: They have to read them the moment they put handcuffs on you.
options.explanation: There is no rule requiring it at the moment of arrest. The warning is tied to questioning you while in custody, not to the handcuffs.

questions.hint: The warning is attached to one specific thing. Is it the arrest, or the questions?
questions.principle: A lot of people believe that if police do not read your rights, the case disappears. That is not how it works. The warning is tied to questioning someone who is in custody, not to the moment of arrest. Officers can arrest you without saying a word, and the arrest is still valid. If they later question you in custody without the warning, your answers may not be usable, but other evidence usually still is. It also does not protect things you say on your own without being asked. Waiting for the warning is not a plan. Saying you want a lawyer works whether or not anyone read you anything.

keyPhrase.quote: No warning does not mean no case.
keyPhrase.gloss: Say you want a lawyer either way. That part always works.

scenario.setup: You are in the back of a patrol car. Nobody has read you anything.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: They never read me my rights. This has to get dropped.

lines.label: OFFICER
lines.text: So what happened back there?

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: I want a lawyer. I am not answering questions.

lines.label: YES
lines.text: You do not have to guess whether the warning was required. Asking for a lawyer works either way.

lines.label: NO
lines.text: You may answer questions expecting them not to count, and a court may decide they do.

scenario.note: Whether the warning was required is something a lawyer sorts out later. It is not something to figure out in the car.

questions.q: An officer stops you outside school and asks questions about your friend, not about you. Do you have to answer?

options.text: No. You can decline to answer questions about anyone, including other people.
Yes. Your rights only cover questions about yourself.
options.explanation: The right to stay silent covers every question, not just questions about you. It does not matter who the question is about.

options.text: Yes, unless you are the one being investigated.
options.explanation: Rights do not switch on only once you become a suspect. You can decline to answer at any point, whatever the questions are about.

options.text: No, but refusing makes you look like you are hiding something.
options.explanation: Choosing not to answer cannot be used against you. Saying you are not sure is also better than guessing, because a wrong detail said confidently can cause real problems for someone else.

questions.hint: Your right covers the questions you get asked. Does it matter whose name is in the question?
questions.principle: Your right to stay quiet covers every question. It is not just about questions about you. If an officer asks about a friend, or about something you saw, you can say no. That is harder than it sounds. Answering feels safe when you are not the one in trouble. But people remember things wrong all the time. A wrong detail can cause real problems for someone else. And a talk that starts about someone else can turn toward you. You can say you do not want to answer, about anyone.

keyPhrase.quote: I don't want to answer questions about anyone.
keyPhrase.gloss: Your rights cover questions about other people too, not just about you.

scenario.setup: You are heading out the side doors after school. An officer is standing by the lot.

lines.label: OFFICER
lines.text: You know Marcus, right? Was he around here yesterday?

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: I don't want to answer questions about anyone.

lines.label: OFFICER
lines.text: You're not in trouble. I just need to know if you saw him.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: I understand. I still don't want to answer questions.

lines.label: YES
lines.text: You did not guess at something you were not sure about, and the conversation stayed short.

lines.label: NO
lines.text: You say "yeah, he was here around four." If that turns out to be wrong, or matters more than you knew, you cannot take it back.

scenario.note: You are allowed to not know, and you are allowed to not say. Neither one is lying.

questions.q: An officer tells you "you're a minor, so you have to answer my questions." Is that correct?

options.text: No. The right to stay silent applies at any age.
Yes. Minors have to answer until a parent gets there.
options.explanation: There is no rule that makes minors answer. The right to stay silent does not wait for a parent to arrive.

options.text: Yes, but only for basic questions like where you live.
options.explanation: Being a minor does not create a category of questions you are required to answer.

options.text: No, but it becomes true once you are actually arrested.
options.explanation: It works the other way. Once you are in custody, the right to stay silent matters more, not less.

questions.hint: Is this a right you get at a certain birthday, or one you already have?
questions.principle: These rights are not something you get when you turn eighteen. A fourteen-year-old has the same right to stay silent and the same right to a lawyer as an adult. Age changes some things in the legal system, but not whether these two rights exist. Courts have also recognized that age matters in a second way: how old you are can affect whether a judge later decides you were being held, because a young person may feel far less free to walk away than an adult would. That works in your favor. It does not make the rights wait until you are older.

keyPhrase.quote: I'm using my right to remain silent, same as anyone.
keyPhrase.gloss: Age does not turn these on or off.

scenario.setup: You are at the bus stop after practice. An officer walks up.

lines.label: OFFICER
lines.text: You're a minor, so you need to answer me.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: I am using my right to remain silent.

lines.label: OFFICER
lines.text: I can call your parents.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: Okay. I am still not answering questions.

lines.label: YES
lines.text: The rights work. Your age did not cancel them.

lines.label: NO
lines.text: You answer everything thinking you had no choice, when you did.

scenario.note: Calling your parents is fine and often a good thing. It does not change your answer.

questions.q: Your family cannot afford a lawyer. What does that mean for you?

options.text: You still get a lawyer, for free, if your family cannot pay.
You have to answer questions until your family can hire someone.
options.explanation: You never have to answer while you wait for anything. Asking for a lawyer works right now, no matter what your family can pay.

options.text: You get a lawyer only if you are charged with something serious.
options.explanation: How serious the charge is does not change it. In juvenile cases you get a lawyer either way.

options.text: You can ask for one, but you will get a bill later.
options.explanation: Worrying about a bill is not a reason to skip asking. Cost is something the court sorts out, not something you decide in the moment.

questions.hint: Which of these turns a right into something you have to buy?
questions.principle: You do not need money to get a lawyer. If your family cannot pay, the court gives you one. That is true in juvenile cases too. The Supreme Court decided this in a case called In re Gault in 1967. Before that, juvenile courts often ran with no lawyer at all. Now young people get one, plus notice of the charges and a chance to question witnesses. Money is not the gate. Ask first and let the court work out who pays.

keyPhrase.quote: I can't pay, and I still want a lawyer.
keyPhrase.gloss: Money is not the gate. Ask and let the court sort it out.

scenario.setup: Kitchen table at home. Your mom is worried about what a lawyer costs.

lines.label: MOM
lines.text: We can't afford a lawyer right now.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: I think the court gives you one if you can't pay.

lines.label: MOM
lines.text: Are you sure?

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: I'm going to ask for one either way.

lines.label: YES
lines.text: The court sorts out who pays. That is not your job to figure out first.

lines.label: NO
lines.text: Questions may keep coming in the meantime, and answers given while waiting still count.

scenario.note: Ask for a lawyer before anyone figures out the money. Those are separate problems.

questions.q: Your mom arrives and tells the officer it is fine for you to answer. Whose decision is it?

options.text: Yours. A parent cannot give up your rights for you.
Your mom's, because you are under 18 and she is responsible for you.
options.explanation: A parent is responsible for a lot of things, but your right to stay silent is not one of them. It belongs to you.

options.text: The officer's, once a parent has agreed.
options.explanation: An officer does not decide whether you use your rights. Nobody in the room can turn them off for you.

options.text: Both of yours together, so you have to agree with her.
options.explanation: You do not need anyone to sign off. You can use your rights even if the adults present want you to talk.

questions.hint: These rights are attached to a person. Which person?
questions.principle: Your rights belong to you, not to your parents. A parent can be there and can help. But they cannot give up your right to stay quiet for you. That surprises people. Parents make almost every other choice for a kid. It works both ways too. Your parent cannot make you talk. And you do not need their okay to ask for a lawyer. If a parent says yes for you and you do not want to answer, say so yourself.

keyPhrase.quote: I still don't want to answer questions.
keyPhrase.gloss: Your rights are yours. Nobody else can spend them.

scenario.setup: The station lobby. Your mom just got there and she is trying to help.

lines.label: MOM
lines.text: He'll talk to you, it's fine, we have nothing to hide.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: I still don't want to answer questions. I want a lawyer.

lines.label: OFFICER
lines.text: Your mom says it's alright.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: I understand. I still don't want to answer questions.

lines.label: YES
lines.text: Your words are the ones that count. The questioning stops on what you said.

lines.label: NO
lines.text: You answer because an adult said it was fine, and those answers are yours, not hers.

scenario.note: This is not disobeying your parent. It is the one decision the law says is yours alone.

questions.q: You and two friends are stopped in a parking lot. One friend starts explaining everything. Does that change your rights?

options.text: No. Your rights are yours, and what someone else says does not use them up.
Yes. Once one of you explains, staying quiet looks worse.
options.explanation: Choosing not to answer cannot be used against you, whatever anyone standing next to you decides to do.

options.text: Yes. If your friend already told the story, there is no point staying quiet.
options.explanation: Their version is their statement. Adding yours gives a second account that can differ in small ways and create new problems.

options.text: No, but you should correct anything your friend gets wrong.
options.explanation: Correcting the story is still talking about the case. You can decline entirely, even if you think something was said wrong.

questions.hint: Whose rights are they? Can somebody else spend them for you?
questions.principle: Your rights belong to you alone. If a friend decides to explain everything, that is their choice and their statement. It does not cancel your right to stay silent, and it does not make your silence look like an admission. This comes up constantly in groups, because once one person starts talking it feels strange to be the only one who does not. Two separate accounts of the same night rarely match perfectly, and the small differences can matter more than anything either person meant to say. You can stay quiet and still be a good friend.

keyPhrase.quote: My friend's choice is not my choice.
keyPhrase.gloss: Your rights are yours. Nobody else can spend them.

scenario.setup: A parking lot behind the store. Three of you, one officer.

lines.label: FRIEND
lines.text: We were just walking through, we didn't take anything, we were only here like ten minutes.

lines.label: OFFICER
lines.text: And you? Same story?

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: I am not answering questions.

lines.label: OFFICER
lines.text: Your friend already explained it.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: I understand. I am still not answering questions.

lines.label: YES
lines.text: There is one account, not two, and none of it came from you.

lines.label: NO
lines.text: You have now made a statement too, and any detail you add or change becomes its own thing.

scenario.note: Staying quiet is not turning on your friend. It is not adding a second version.

questions.q: You say you want a lawyer. What actually happens next?

options.text: Questions about the case stop, but you may still be held.
You get released and go home.
options.explanation: Asking for a lawyer stops the questioning. It does not decide whether you are held or let go, which is a separate decision.

options.text: A lawyer shows up in the room within a few minutes.
options.explanation: It usually takes longer than that. The important part is that questioning has to stop in the meantime.

options.text: Nothing happens unless you have already been charged.
options.explanation: You do not have to wait for charges. Asking works during questioning, which is usually before any charge exists.

questions.hint: One thing stops right away. A lot of other things keep moving.
questions.principle: Here is the honest version, because not knowing is a big reason people never ask. When you clearly say you want a lawyer, questions about the case have to stop. That is the part that happens right away. What does not happen is everything else. You are not automatically released, a lawyer does not appear in seconds, and the case does not end. You might still be held while decisions get made by other people. That can feel like asking did not work. It did work. The point of asking is not to end the day faster. It is to make sure nothing else gets added to the case while you wait.

keyPhrase.quote: I want a lawyer.
keyPhrase.gloss: The questions stop. Everything else takes the time it takes.

scenario.setup: A small office at school. An officer and an administrator are both there.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: I want a lawyer. I am not answering questions.

lines.label: OFFICER
lines.text: Alright. We'll stop there.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: Nothing else is happening. Did that even work?

lines.label: YES
lines.text: It worked. Questioning stopped. The waiting is normal and it is not a sign you did the wrong thing.

lines.label: NO
lines.text: You might give up and start talking again because it felt like nothing changed, which undoes the protection you just got.

scenario.note: Asking for a lawyer protects the case, not the schedule.

questions.q: Your dad is upset and tells you to just explain everything so this can be over. What is the best thing to say?

options.text: "I want to talk to a lawyer first."
"Okay, I'll tell them everything."
options.explanation: Explaining because a parent is upset is still explaining. The pressure makes sense. The statement still lasts forever.

options.text: "I'll leave out the part that looks bad."
options.explanation: Half a story is still a statement, and the missing part usually comes out later anyway.

options.text: "You talk to them for me."
options.explanation: A parent cannot answer for you, and what they repeat can become part of the case too.

questions.hint: Who is the one person in this situation whose job is to advise you?
questions.principle: Parents want this over with, and that is love, not bad advice from a bad person. But a parent is not a lawyer, and "just explain it" is the most common piece of well meant advice that makes a case worse. You can respect your parent and still wait for a lawyer. Saying so out loud is not disrespect. It also helps to tell your parent why: not because you did something, but because a statement cannot be taken back and a lawyer is the person who knows what is safe to say.

keyPhrase.quote: I want to talk to a lawyer first.
keyPhrase.gloss: You can love your parents and still wait.

scenario.setup: Your living room. Your dad is pacing and wants this handled tonight.

lines.label: DAD
lines.text: Just tell them what happened. You didn't do anything, so say it.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: I want to talk to a lawyer first.

lines.label: DAD
lines.text: That makes it look like you did something.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: It doesn't. Everyone gets one. I just don't want to say the wrong thing.

lines.label: YES
lines.text: You wait for the person whose job is knowing what is safe to say.

lines.label: NO
lines.text: You explain to calm the room down, and that explanation stays in the case.

scenario.note: Your parent is on your side. A lawyer is the one who knows what to do with that.

questions.q: An officer hands you a pen and asks you to write it down instead of saying it. What is true about a written statement?

options.text: It counts the same as saying it out loud.
It is safer, because you control exactly what it says.
options.explanation: Controlling the wording does not make it less usable. A statement in your own handwriting is often stronger evidence, not weaker.

options.text: It does not count unless you sign it.
options.explanation: A statement counts whether or not you sign it. The signature is not what makes it real.

options.text: A statement without a warning first is not worth anything.
options.explanation: What you write can count regardless. Whether a warning was required is something a lawyer sorts out later.

questions.hint: Does the form the words take change what they are?
questions.principle: Writing it down is not a safer way to talk. A written statement is still a statement. In some ways it is stronger, because it is in your own words and your own handwriting. Signing it does not matter. Neither does typing it or texting it. People feel better about writing because they pick the words. But the words are the part that gets used. If you decided not to answer questions, that covers writing too.

keyPhrase.quote: I'm not writing a statement either.
keyPhrase.gloss: Saying it and writing it are the same thing.

scenario.setup: A room at school. An administrator slides a form across the table.

lines.label: STAFF
lines.text: Just write down your version so we have it on paper.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: I'm not writing a statement.

lines.label: STAFF
lines.text: It's for your own protection.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: I understand. I still want to talk to a lawyer first.

lines.label: YES
lines.text: There is no document with your account on it, and nothing to be read back later.

lines.label: NO
lines.text: Your version now exists in your own handwriting, and it cannot be edited or taken back.

scenario.note: A blank page is not an admission. It is just a blank page.

questions.q: You are held at a facility and call your friend from the phone there. What is true about that call?

options.text: It is generally recorded and could be listened to later.
It is private, since nobody is questioning you.
options.explanation: It is not about who you call. Calls from these places get recorded either way.

options.text: It is private as long as you do not talk about the case directly.
options.explanation: The recording happens no matter what you say. Talking around it still leaves a recording someone can read into.

options.text: It is recorded, but a recorded call cannot be used as evidence.
options.explanation: Recorded calls have been used as proof in court. Being recorded is what makes them usable.

questions.hint: The question is about the phone, not about what you say into it.
questions.principle: Phone calls from a jail are almost always recorded. Those recordings can be used later. This surprises people. Calling a friend feels private in a way a small room does not. It is not. A notice usually plays at the start, but people stop hearing it. There is one exception. Calls with your lawyer are meant to be private. Treat every other call as one someone may hear. If you want to talk about what happened, save it for your lawyer.

keyPhrase.quote: I can't get into it on this phone.
keyPhrase.gloss: Only lawyer calls are private.

scenario.setup: A phone on the wall. Your friend picks up.

lines.label: FRIEND
lines.text: are you okay?? what happened

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: I can't get into it on this phone.

lines.label: FRIEND
lines.text: why not

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: it's recorded. I'll tell you later.

lines.label: YES
lines.text: The recording exists, but there is nothing on it about the case.

lines.label: NO
lines.text: Your account is now a recording that other people can listen to.

scenario.note: Calls with your lawyer are different. Those are meant to be private.

questions.q: Courts have said your age matters when deciding if you were being held. Why does that help you?

options.text: Because a young person can feel unable to leave in a situation where an adult would not.
Because minors get a warning that adults do not get.
options.explanation: The warning is the same. What differs is how a judge weighs the situation you were in.

options.text: Because statements by minors are never allowed in court.
options.explanation: Statements by young people are used all the time. Age is one factor a judge weighs, not an automatic block.

options.text: Because officers have to treat minors more gently.
options.explanation: This is about how a judge looks back at the situation later, not about a rule for how officers behave.

questions.hint: The question is not what an officer must do. It is what a judge decides a situation felt like.
questions.principle: The Supreme Court decided a case called J.D.B. v. North Carolina. It says your age counts when a judge decides if you were being held. The reason is simple. A fourteen-year-old with adults in charge all around may feel stuck. A grown adult in the same spot might just walk away. Michigan courts use this too, including at school. It helps you, because more situations can count as being held. But it does not decide anything in the moment. Asking if you are free to leave still does.

keyPhrase.quote: Am I being detained?
keyPhrase.gloss: Same question as free to leave. Either one works.

scenario.setup: Sitting in the back of a friend's car, parked. An officer is at the window with a flashlight.

lines.label: OFFICER
lines.text: Everybody stay where you are. I've got some questions.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: Am I free to leave?

lines.label: OFFICER
lines.text: No. Sit tight.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: I am using my right to remain silent. I want a lawyer.

lines.label: YES
lines.text: You said the words at the moment it turned into being held.

lines.label: NO
lines.text: You answer because nobody said the word custody, and the answers count.

scenario.note: You will not know at the time whether a judge would call it custody. Asking and staying silent works either way.

questions.q: An officer asks what time you saw something happen. You think it was around nine but you are not certain. What should you say?

options.text: "I'm not sure, and I don't want to guess."
"Around nine, I think."
options.explanation: A guess sounds like a fact once it is written down. If it was actually seven, that wrong time is now in the file with your name attached.

options.text: "Nine."
options.explanation: Saying it flat makes a shaky memory sound sure. Other people may then treat it as fact.

options.text: "I don't know, but it was definitely after dark."
options.explanation: Adding a detail is still adding a detail. That new piece can be wrong the same way a time can.

questions.hint: Which answer stays true no matter what really happened?
questions.principle: Not knowing is a full answer. Memory is shaky about the things officers ask about. Times, order, and who was where are the hardest to get right. A detail you give to be helpful can be wrong. A wrong detail is hard to take back once it is written down. Other people may build on it. Saying you are not sure cannot be proven wrong, because you did not claim anything. It also does not make you look guilty. Not guessing is not the same as not helping.

keyPhrase.quote: I'm not sure, and I don't want to guess.
keyPhrase.gloss: Not knowing is an answer. Guessing is a statement.

scenario.setup: Outside the gym after a game. An officer is asking about something that happened in the parking lot.

lines.label: OFFICER
lines.text: What time did you see them out there?

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: I'm not sure, and I don't want to guess.

lines.label: OFFICER
lines.text: Roughly. Nine? Ten?

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: I really don't know.

lines.label: YES
lines.text: Nothing you said can turn out to be wrong, because you did not claim anything.

lines.label: NO
lines.text: You say nine. If it was actually seven, that time is now in the file with your name on it.

scenario.note: Being helpful and being accurate are not always the same thing.

questions.q: What does it mean to be "in custody" for the purposes of your rights?

options.text: That a reasonable person would not feel free to leave.
That you have been handcuffed.
options.explanation: Handcuffs are one sign, but you can be in custody without them and handcuffed without being questioned.

options.text: That the questions are happening inside a police station.
options.explanation: It depends on the situation, not the building. It can happen on a sidewalk, in a car, or at school.

options.text: That an officer has told you that you are in custody.
options.explanation: There is no announcement. It is decided later by looking at the whole situation.

questions.hint: It is about how the moment would feel, not about a word or an object.
questions.principle: "In custody" does not mean handcuffs, and it does not mean being at a station. It means a reasonable person in your situation would not feel free to end things and walk away. A judge decides that later by looking at everything: where you were, how many officers, how long, what was said. It matters because custody plus questioning is what triggers the warning. There is one part that helps you: courts have said a young person's age counts in this, because a fifteen-year-old may feel much less free to leave than an adult would in the same spot. You do not have to work this out yourself. Ask if you are free to leave.

keyPhrase.quote: Am I free to leave, or am I being detained?
keyPhrase.gloss: You do not have to figure out custody. Just ask.

scenario.setup: A hallway at school. Two officers, and the door is shut.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: Am I free to leave?

lines.label: OFFICER
lines.text: Not right now.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: I am using my right to remain silent. I want a lawyer.

lines.label: YES
lines.text: You learn where you stand without needing to know any legal terms.

lines.label: NO
lines.text: You may assume it is casual because there are no handcuffs, and answer everything.

scenario.note: No handcuffs does not mean free to go. The answer to the question does.

questions.q: A school officer pulls you out of class to ask about something that happened off campus. Do your rights apply?

options.text: Yes. A school officer is still an officer.
No. Anything said to school staff stays at school.
options.explanation: What you say to a school officer can leave the school and end up in a case.

options.text: No, because school rules replace your rights during the school day.
options.explanation: School rules can govern discipline, but they do not remove your right to stay silent or ask for a lawyer.

options.text: Yes, but only if the officer is in uniform.
options.explanation: A uniform is not what matters. It depends on who they are and what they are doing.

questions.hint: Does the building someone works in change what they are?
questions.principle: A school resource officer is a police officer who works at a school. That is easy to forget. You see them every day and they may be friendly, which is a good thing. But when they ask about something that could become a case, your rights work the same. School discipline and a court case are two different tracks. One talk can feed both. It is not rude to say you want a lawyer or a parent first. You can be polite and still not answer.

keyPhrase.quote: Can I call my parents first?
keyPhrase.gloss: Being at school does not change who you are talking to.

scenario.setup: Pulled out of third hour. A school officer you know by name.

lines.label: SRO
lines.text: You're not in trouble. I just want to hear your side about Saturday.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: I want to talk to my parents and a lawyer first.

lines.label: SRO
lines.text: This is just between us.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: I understand. I'd still like to talk to them first.

lines.label: YES
lines.text: Nothing you said travels, because you did not say anything.

lines.label: NO
lines.text: What you said can go beyond the school and into a case.

scenario.note: Knowing an officer and being off the record with them are two different things.

questions.q: You are a passenger in a car that gets pulled over. What are you actually required to do?

options.text: Follow instructions, and possibly give your name, but not answer questions about a case.
Answer everything the officer asks, the same as the driver.
options.explanation: A traffic stop is about the driving. It does not put every passenger under an obligation to answer questions about a case.

options.text: Answer, because you are in someone else's car.
options.explanation: Being a passenger does not give you the driver's responsibilities. Whose car it is does not decide your rights.

options.text: Nothing at all, and you can walk away whenever you want.
options.explanation: You may be required to stay while the stop is happening, and officers can tell people to stay in or step out of the car. Not answering is different from leaving.

questions.hint: Two different things: what you must do with your body, and what you must say.
questions.principle: A traffic stop is about the driver and the driving. As a passenger, you may have to stay while it happens. An officer can tell you to stay in the car or step out. Do what they say. In some states you may also have to give your name. Giving your name is not the same as being interviewed. You do not have to answer anything past that. People mix those two up all the time. You can follow every order, give your name, and still not answer questions.

keyPhrase.quote: I'll do what you ask. I'm not answering questions.
keyPhrase.gloss: Follow instructions with your body. Keep your rights with your words.

scenario.setup: Passenger seat, late evening. Your friend got pulled over for a taillight.

lines.label: OFFICER
lines.text: Where are you two headed?

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: I'm not answering questions.

lines.label: OFFICER
lines.text: Step out of the vehicle please.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: Okay. I'm still not answering questions.

lines.label: YES
lines.text: You cooperate with the stop and nothing about a case comes from you.

lines.label: NO
lines.text: You turn a taillight stop into a much bigger problem for yourself.

scenario.note: Doing what you are told and staying silent are not in conflict. Do both.

questions.q: Officers knock on your door and ask to come in and talk. Do you have to open it?

options.text: No. You can talk through the door or say you would rather not.
Yes. Refusing to open the door is against the law.
options.explanation: You usually do not have to open your door. Police need a warrant or another legal reason to come in.

options.text: Only when there is no adult in the house with you.
options.explanation: Whether an adult is home does not create a duty to open the door.

options.text: No, but if you open it, anything said is just a friendly conversation.
options.explanation: A conversation at your door is like any other conversation with police. It can be used the same way.

questions.hint: There are two choices here. Opening a door is one. Answering is the other.
questions.principle: You usually do not have to open your door for police. They need a warrant or another legal reason to come in. You also do not have to answer questions through the door. Two things people miss. A talk at the door counts the same as any other talk. And stepping outside can change things. If you are home alone and under eighteen, it is fine to say you want to wait for a parent. That is not refusing to help. It is asking for the adult who should be there.

keyPhrase.quote: I'd rather wait until my parents are home.
keyPhrase.gloss: A closed door is an answer. So is not answering.

scenario.setup: Home alone after school. A knock at the front door.

lines.label: OFFICER
lines.text: Can we come in and talk for a minute?

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: I'd rather wait until my parents are home.

lines.label: OFFICER
lines.text: It'll only take a second.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: I'd still rather wait until they're here.

lines.label: YES
lines.text: Nothing happens that a parent is not part of.

lines.label: NO
lines.text: A conversation you did not have to have becomes part of the record.

scenario.note: If officers say they have a warrant, do not fight about it at the door. Step aside, stay quiet, and let a lawyer handle it later.

questions.q: You are stopped and you are sure the officer has no good reason. What is the best thing to do right now?

options.text: Stay calm, follow instructions, and say you are not answering questions.
Explain why the stop is not allowed and refuse to cooperate until they admit it.
options.explanation: The street is not where that gets decided. Arguing it out usually makes the stop longer and can create a new charge.

options.text: Walk away, since an unlawful stop does not count.
options.explanation: Walking away from a stop can be its own crime. That stays true even if the stop was not proper.

options.text: Record it and tell the officer nothing they do counts now.
options.explanation: You may be allowed to record. But saying nothing counts does not make it so, and it tends to heat things up.

questions.hint: There are two places to fight this. Which one has a judge in it?
questions.principle: Being right about a stop and winning right now are two different things. If a stop was not proper, a judge sorts that out later. A lawyer can argue to keep evidence out. What almost never works is fighting about it on the street. It can add charges that did not exist a minute ago. It can also make a short stop long. The best thing you can do is stay calm, do what you are told, say you are not answering, and remember details. Your objection is worth more later.

keyPhrase.quote: I'll sort this out later, with a lawyer.
keyPhrase.gloss: Win it in court, not on the street.

scenario.setup: Stopped while walking home. You do not think there was any reason for it.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: This isn't right. He can't just stop me.

lines.label: OFFICER
lines.text: Keep your hands where I can see them.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: Okay. I'm not answering questions.

lines.label: YES
lines.text: The stop ends sooner and your objection is still available later, in a place where it counts.

lines.label: NO
lines.text: The stop gets longer, and something new can be added that had nothing to do with why you were stopped.

scenario.note: Being right is worth a lot. It is worth the most in court.

questions.q: A vice principal, not an officer, asks you to explain what happened. What is true about that conversation?

options.text: It is not a police interview, but what you say can still reach a case.
A vice principal cannot be asked about it later.
options.explanation: School staff can be asked what you told them, and school reports can end up in a case.

options.text: It is exactly the same as being questioned by police.
options.explanation: It is not identical. School discipline runs on its own rules, and a warning is not required the way it can be with police.

options.text: You are required to answer because school rules say to cooperate.
options.explanation: School rules can lead to discipline, but they cannot make you give a statement that could be used against you in a case.

questions.hint: Two different systems can care about the same talk.
questions.principle: School rules and a court case are two systems. One talk can reach both. A vice principal asking what happened is usually about school rules. Saying no can lead to school consequences like detention. That is real. Also real: a staff member can be asked later what you told them. If it could become a case, ask to talk to your parents and a lawyer first. That is fair, even at school. You can be polite about everything except the details.

keyPhrase.quote: Can I talk to my parents before I answer?
keyPhrase.gloss: School rules and a court case are two systems. One conversation can reach both.

scenario.setup: The vice principal's office. No officer, just her and the door closed.

lines.label: STAFF
lines.text: I just need your side of what happened at lunch.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: Can I talk to my parents before I answer?

lines.label: STAFF
lines.text: This is a school matter, not a police thing.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: I understand. I'd still like to talk to them first.

lines.label: YES
lines.text: You may still face school consequences, but nothing you said can travel into a case.

lines.label: NO
lines.text: Your account exists, and a staff member can be asked about it later.

scenario.note: Asking for your parents is not refusing to cooperate. Say it politely and stick to it.

questions.q: You already said you were not answering questions, but the officer keeps asking. What should you do?

options.text: Say it again, calmly, as many times as you need to.
Answer this one, since you already made your point.
options.explanation: One answer restarts the conversation. Everything after it counts, no matter what you said earlier.

options.text: Say nothing at all now, since you already said it once.
options.explanation: Staying quiet is safer than talking. Saying it out loud again is better, because then nobody can argue you meant something else.

options.text: Tell them they are not allowed to keep asking and that you will report it.
options.explanation: Threats tend to heat things up without helping. Saying the same calm words does more.

questions.hint: What is the least dramatic thing that keeps working?
questions.principle: Saying it once is enough under the law. In real life, people get asked again anyway. Sometimes in different words. Sometimes after a break. The best answer is to repeat yourself calmly. That is not rude and it does not weaken you. What weakens you is answering one more question because you are worn down. That one answer can count as choosing to talk again. Saying the same words the same way also removes any argument later.

keyPhrase.quote: Same answer, every time.
keyPhrase.gloss: Repeat it calmly. That is the whole technique.

scenario.setup: Twenty minutes in. Same room, same questions in a different order.

lines.label: OFFICER
lines.text: Let's try this again. Where were you?

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: I'm still not answering questions.

lines.label: OFFICER
lines.text: You know this looks bad, right?

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: I'm still not answering questions.

lines.label: YES
lines.text: Nothing new comes from you, and there is no argument later about whether you meant it.

lines.label: NO
lines.text: That one counts, and it can be treated as deciding to talk again.

scenario.note: Repeating yourself is not being difficult. It is the whole technique.

questions.q: An officer says you can go home as soon as you answer one more question. What is the problem with that trade?

options.text: The officer questioning you does not decide whether you go home.
There is no problem. One question is not much, and then it is over.
options.explanation: One more question is rarely one more question, and the last answer is often the one that matters most.

options.text: One short answer cannot hurt, so keeping it brief is enough.
options.explanation: Short answers still count. A single sentence can place you somewhere or confirm something.

options.text: The only problem is that the promise is not in writing.
options.explanation: A promise like that would not bind a prosecutor or a judge anyway, so a written version does not fix anything.

questions.hint: Look at who is offering the deal and ask whether they own the thing being offered.
questions.principle: "Just one more question and you can go" is a hard thing to hear when you want to go home. Here is why it is not a trade worth taking. The officer in the room does not decide whether charges get filed, and often does not decide when you leave. Those decisions belong to other people, later. Meanwhile the answer you give is permanent. Research shows the wish to get out of the room is one of the biggest reasons young people give up their rights. Wanting to go home is completely normal. It is just not something you can buy with an answer.

keyPhrase.quote: Not one more question.
keyPhrase.gloss: Not a short one either.

scenario.setup: Late. You are tired and you want to go home.

lines.label: OFFICER
lines.text: One question and we're done. Were you there or not?

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: I'm not answering any questions.

lines.label: OFFICER
lines.text: That's all I need and you can walk out.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: I'm not answering any questions.

lines.label: YES
lines.text: Whether you go home gets decided by other people, and nothing was added to the case.

lines.label: NO
lines.text: You may not go home anyway, and now the answer exists.

scenario.note: If it really is one question, it will still be there tomorrow with a lawyer next to you.

questions.q: You asked for a lawyer and one is coming. What is a lawyer actually there to do?

options.text: Give you advice about what to say and make sure the rules are followed.
Prove you are innocent right there in the room.
options.explanation: That is not what happens in a questioning room. A lawyer protects your position now and argues the case later.

options.text: Speak for you so you can go home faster.
options.explanation: A lawyer is not a shortcut home. Whether you are released is decided separately.

options.text: Tell the officers they cannot use anything they already have.
options.explanation: A lawyer can argue later that certain evidence should not be allowed, but that is a court argument, not something declared in the room.

questions.hint: Is a lawyer there to end the day, or to protect what happens next?
questions.principle: A lawyer is not a magic word. Knowing what they do makes it easier to ask. Their job is to tell you what is safe to say. They make sure the rules are followed. They speak for you later. They are also the only person you can talk to with real privacy. Not a friend, not a group chat, not a recorded call. What they are not is a fast way home. They do not end the case on the spot. Asking for one is not admitting anything.

keyPhrase.quote: I'd rather wait for my lawyer.
keyPhrase.gloss: Their job starts before court, not at it.

scenario.setup: Waiting. Your parent is next to you and nobody has said much.

lines.label: MOM
lines.text: Do you really need a lawyer? It makes it seem like you did something.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: It doesn't. Everyone gets one.

lines.label: MOM
lines.text: Okay. We'll wait then.

lines.label: YES
lines.text: You get advice before you say anything, which is the point.

lines.label: NO
lines.text: You give up the one protection that works before court.

scenario.note: Asking for a lawyer is not an admission. It is what the process expects you to do.

questions.q: An officer stops you and starts asking questions. What is the order that protects you best?

options.text: Ask if you are free to leave, then say you are staying silent and want a lawyer.
Explain what happened first, then ask for a lawyer if it gets serious.
options.explanation: By the time it feels serious, the explanation already exists. The protection has to come first.

options.text: Stay completely silent from the start and say nothing at all.
options.explanation: Silence alone does not turn the right on. You have to say you are using it.

options.text: Ask for a lawyer first, then answer anything that seems harmless while you wait.
options.explanation: Asking only works if you also stop talking. Answering while you wait undoes it.

questions.hint: Find out where you stand, then say the words, then stop.
questions.principle: Put it together and it is short. First, find out where you stand: "Am I free to leave?" If yes, you can go. If no, say the words out loud: "I am using my right to remain silent. I want a lawyer." Then stop talking, and repeat it calmly if the questions keep coming. Do what you are told with your body the whole time. That is the entire thing. It works at fourteen and at forty, on a sidewalk, in a car, at school, or at a station. You do not need to know legal terms or figure out whether you are in custody. You need three sentences and the patience to repeat them.

keyPhrase.quote: Am I free to leave? I am using my right to remain silent. I want a lawyer.
keyPhrase.gloss: Three sentences, in that order. That is the whole plan.

scenario.setup: Anywhere. A sidewalk, a car, a school hallway. It always looks like this.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: Am I free to leave?

lines.label: OFFICER
lines.text: No, not yet.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: I am using my right to remain silent. I want a lawyer.

lines.label: OFFICER
lines.text: Just tell me one thing first.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: I am using my right to remain silent.

lines.label: YES
lines.text: You know where you stand, the rights are on, and nothing new comes from you.

lines.label: NO
lines.text: You end up explaining first and protecting yourself second, which is backwards.

scenario.note: You will not remember a court case under stress. You can remember three sentences.
